newsitem.title: USA: Demand seen leading force behind U.S. growth-Guynn.
newsitem.headline: Demand seen leading force behind U.S. growth-Guynn.

text.p: Strength in consumer spending has been the leading force behind the current U.S. economic expansion, said Jack Guynn, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

"It now looks like 1997 is likely to exceed last year's 2-1/2 percent annualized growth. Where's the strength behind this growth? Consumer spending is leading the way," Guynn told a Chamber of Commerce luncheon in Murfreesboro.

"We've all seen the reports of month-after-month strong job growth -- and income growth has been strong as well," Guynn said, adding that, "If the savings rate falls again, or we see consumers starting to spend more on the basis of their perceived growth, this would be a concern."
Guynn said consumer demand currently presents the largest upside risk to the U.S. economy.
"I would point out that the largest upside risk is in the area of consumer demand, which accounts for about two-thirds of GDP (Gross Domestic Product)," Guynn said.
The Atlanta Fed president said he sees continued moderate growth in 1997. He added, however, that some slowing in the economy was expected as the year progresses.

"We're now nearly one-third of the way through 1997, and most of us expect to see continued moderate growth -- with low inflation and low unemployment. But most of us also expect to begin seeing some slowing in the pace of activity as we move through 1997," Guynn said.
The Atlanta Fed chief said the housing sector was also expected to slow in the upcoming months.
"We're expecting some slowing in housing over the rest of 1997 and into 1998," Guynn said.
The Atlanta Fed chief said labor availability was one of the sectors under the most pressure during the current economic cycle, which has entered its seventh year of expansion.
Guynn also stressed the central bank's need to be preemptive against inflationary pressures, adding that the Fed cannot wait for months of deteriorating inflation data.
"Essentially the Fed has to do its best to look months ahead and take preemptive actions against the possibility of accelerating inflation," Guynn said.
He added that the Fed must "always keep its eye on the inflation ball."
